name: Sensor and Shipping Data
title: Sensor and Shipping Data
answer: Sensor and shipping data covers the digital exhaust of physical movement: vessel positions from AIS, port call records, container and bulk cargo manifests where available, terminal gate and crane activity, truck and rail telematics, and fixed or mobile IoT sensors on assets and in facilities. It also includes satellite and aerial imagery used to count vessels, tanks, containers, or activity at ports and industrial sites. In alternative data terms, these feeds are used to build high-frequency indicators of trade, supply chain stress, commodity flows, and industrial activity. The scope spans raw signals, reference data such as vessel registries and port codes, and derived metrics like dwell time, congestion, and route deviation.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of space and terrestrial infrastructure: satellite constellations and ground stations for imagery and AIS, coastal and terrestrial receivers for vessel signals, cellular and low-power networks for IoT devices, and port or carrier systems for operational records. Data lands in cloud object storage and is moved through stream processing and batch pipelines, often with a message queue for live feeds. Reference data services supply vessel identities, ownership links, port codes, and geofences. Analysts and data scientists then access curated tables or APIs from notebooks, dashboards, or production services.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by normalizing timestamps, coordinates, and identifiers, then clean and deduplicate signals, because AIS and sensor feeds contain gaps, noise, and misreports. Geofencing and map matching turn raw points into port calls, berth events, anchorage waits, and route segments. Vessel or asset identity resolution links messages to a registry record, which lets analysts aggregate activity by owner, operator, flag, or fleet. Feature engineering produces metrics such as transit time, congestion, and unusual loitering, which feed time series models, nowcasting, and machine learning classifiers. Validation uses independent sources, historical backtests, and manual review of edge cases before a signal is published.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk start with the terms attached to each feed: AIS and satellite imagery have different licensing, redistribution, and attribution rules, and port or carrier data is often governed by commercial contracts. Privacy and security obligations apply when sensor data can identify individuals, such as truck drivers or terminal workers, and data protection rules may restrict retention or cross-border transfer. Provenance matters because spoofing, jamming, dark vessels, and misconfigured sensors can corrupt a signal, so pipelines need source tracking, versioning, and audit logs. Sanctions and export controls can also apply when vessel or cargo data is used for screening, which makes entity resolution and false positive handling a compliance concern. Teams typically document lineage, quality checks, and permitted uses so that downstream users can judge fitness for purpose.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward denser satellite coverage, cheaper edge sensors, and more frequent updates, which pushes latency from daily to near real time. Fusion with other alternative data, such as weather, energy, and trade records, is becoming common for supply chain and commodity monitoring. Expect more automated quality control, because spoofing and signal loss remain persistent problems, and more demand for explainable derived metrics rather than raw feeds. Regulatory attention to data rights and to the use of location data is likely to shape what can be collected, shared, and resold. The practical direction is toward standardized event schemas and APIs that let non specialists consume shipping and sensor signals without rebuilding the pipeline.
